records.toxicity_detail: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/iris-ensata/), "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: "CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Nausea, salivation, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, diarrhea, elevated temperature following ingestion; skin irritation upon contact with seeds, rootstock, or cell sap." The severity rating comes from that Poisonous to Humans heading. NC State's separate Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses; it gives no pet-specific symptom list or severity. The Plant Type field on the same page lists Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Poisonous and Water Plant, and the tags include #poisonous, #problem for dogs, #problem for cats, #problem for horses and #contact dermatitis. RHS (Iris ensata page), Potentially harmful: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants" RHS's pets line names no animal, so it is not used as cat/dog evidence. toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs entries. soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State's Acid (<6.0) is an open-ended band and RHS gives only the word Acid with no number.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's human-scoped Poison block for this exact species page: "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." Plant Type (same page): Annual, Herbaceous Perennial. NC State's separate tag list carries "#problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats" (tags, not a severity rating; they name dogs, horses and cats without a symptom list). NC State also lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses in its structured Problems field. RHS (species page, Potentially harmful): 'Humans/Pets: Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants'. RHS's Humans/Pets line names no animal. No preparation instruction or edibility statement appears on either page. MoBot gives no toxicity information.
unknowns: MoBot's plantfinder page could not be read through the Bash fetcher (host refuses non-browser clients); it was read in the browser pane. Its quotes may show SKIP in the mechanical check.

NC State's description calls the plant 'a cultivar' and says it 'reaches up to 15" in height'; size here uses NC State's structured Dimensions block (12-18 in height and width) as the anchor. MoBot's structured line reads 'Spread: 1.00 to 1.50 feet' and its prose says it 'typically grows 1-2' (infrequently to 3') tall', and RHS says Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in). Sources differ on the upper height end.

is_houseplant false: NC State treats it as an outdoor border and bedding plant (Plant Type Annual, Herbaceous Perennial; USDA zones 3a-7b), and no admissible source addresses indoor culture. NC State's Landscape Location does list Container, and its prose says "This 'filler' plant makes a good choice for your 'spiller-thriller-filler' container." That is an outdoor container planting, not a houseplant framing.

water_regime null: MoBot's structured Water: Medium is mid-scale and its Culture says 'medium moisture, well-drained'; RHS says moist but well-drained; no watering instruction exists. No day interval or dry-down target is stated.
soil_ph left null: NC State gives Neutral (6.0-8.0) but RHS accepts Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so neither a floor nor a ceiling is supported.
humidity_need left null: NC State tags it 'humidity intolerant' and MoBot says it dislikes the heat and humidity of the deep South, but neither gives a humidity figure or indoor humidity guidance.

Afternoon shade ('Appreciates some afternoon shade' on MoBot; NC State 'provide some shade in the afternoon') is conditional and is not added to outdoor_sun_exposure; all three structured sun fields say full sun.
fertilize fields null: MoBot says 'Fertilize regularly' and NC State 'Fertilize often' with no interval, strength or months.

is_edible false: RHS states "Harmful if eaten." (scoped Humans/Pets) and NC State's Poison block lists the leaves as the poisonous part at medium severity. No admissible source says any part is eaten.
No temperature, chill damage or direct-sun-hour figures stated for this species; NC State hardiness zones 3a-7b, MoBot zone 4 to 7 are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.
Not to be confused with Delphinium elatum (Bee Delphinium) or the annual Consolida ajacis; no cross-species claim is made here.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Tradescantia virginiana. Under the page's 'Poisonous to Humans' heading (human-scoped): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: 'Most species of Tradescantia tend to be mildly toxic to humans and pets if ingested. They may cause mouth and stomach irritation. Handling the leaves or sap of this plant can cause skin irritation, redness, and itching in both humans and pets.' Poison Toxic Principle: unknown, possibly oxalate crystals. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Leaves, Sap/Juice. Separately, the page's Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs; these cat and dog tags are distinct from the human-scoped Poison block. The page's full tag run is: #pollinator plant #native wildflower #NC Native Pollinator Plant #fall flowers #white flowers #summer flowers #NC native #blue flowers #spring flowers #purple flowers #food source nectar #food source pollen #food source summer #Coastal FAC #FACU Piedmont Mountains #border front #pond margins #HS302 #Audubon #Guilford Crevice Garden #wet soils tolerant #problem for dogs #problem for cats #contact dermatitis #poisonous if ingested #problem for children #HS304 #edible flowers. Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Wildflower. Description prose: 'The Virginia spiderwort is reportedly both edible and poisonous. Most species of Tradescantia are mildly toxic to humans and pets, if ingested. They also tend to cause skin irritation upon contact. Exercise caution before eating any part of a wild plant and wear protective gloves when handling this plant.' Edibility is a separate field on the same page: 'Leaves can be eaten raw mixed in salads. Teas can be made from the plant. Flowers are edible.' The page also carries the tag #edible flowers. The toxicity and edibility statements are both reported as the source gives them and the conflict between them is not resolved here.
unknowns: Only plants.ces.ncsu.edu had a readable dedicated page for Tradescantia virginiana. Attempts at missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org failed to connect, RHS tradescantia-virginiana returned 404, Clemson returned 403 and UMD returned 404; no other admissible page was confirmed, so every field rests on NC State alone.
is_houseplant false: NC State treats it as a native landscape perennial (Landscape Location Meadow, Naturalized Area, Pond, Woodland), and no admissible source addresses houseplant use.

Edibility and toxicity conflict on the NC State page (edible leaves and flowers versus low-severity poisonous if ingested, leaves and sap, contact dermatitis yes); is_edible is true only on the source's own edibility statement and the conflict is deliberately left unresolved. The page itself says 'reportedly both edible and poisonous' and advises caution before eating any part of a wild plant.

toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags; the Poison Symptoms sentence about 'pets' names no animal and the severity rating (Low) comes from the human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band is the only pH field and no RHS page was readable to check whether alkaline soils are acceptable; soil_ph_min 6.0 is the stated floor of that band, and the page does not list the Acid band.

water_regime left null: NC State says it 'prefers moist to wet fertile sites' and 'Provide the plant with additional water during dry periods', which is a site preference and a supplemental-water remark, not a watering regime; its tags also say wet soils tolerant and Resistance To Challenges lists Dry Soil and Wet Soil. soil_drainage moderate reads the structured Good Drainage + Moist + Occasionally Wet fields.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Deep shade, Full sun and Partial Shade (mapped to full_shade, full_sun, part_shade); the hours in those labels are the site-wide legend and were not used, so direct_sun_hours_max is null.

chill_damage_f null: 'winter hardy in zones 4 to 9' is a hardiness rating, not a damage-onset temperature. Temperature, humidity, light footcandle, fertilizer and day-interval watering fields are null because no admissible source gives them for this in-ground perennial.
Nothing from Tradescantia zebrina ('Spiderwort / Inch Plant'), Tradescantia fluminensis ('Small-Leaf Spiderwort') or the Tradescantia genus was borrowed for any field.

records.name_note: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list for Heuchera villosa is alphabetized and its first entry is Crag-Jangle, not Hairy Alumroot, but NC State's description leads with 'Hairy alumroot' (one word). MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose and RHS's subtitle write the name as two words, 'hairy alum root'. Hairy Alumroot was chosen as the name NC State's dedicated page uses in its description lead; the spelling differs between sources.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: the NC State page for Heuchera villosa carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and neither the MoBot nor the RHS page for this species addresses toxicity. No dedicated page on the other admissible domains was found.
is_edible is null: no admissible source addresses eating this plant.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's structured Light field lists Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade (mapped to part_shade). MoBot's Sun line and Culture prose say full sun to part shade, but NC State and RHS both exclude full sun, so full_sun is left out (MoBot's 'Performs well in full sun in cooler climates' is also conditional). RHS's Position field lists Full shade, Partial shade, but NC State and MoBot do not list full shade, so full_shade is left out. part_sun is not added because NC State's Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: NC State's '2-6 hours' is the site-wide light-category legend text, and no species-specific prose gives an hour figure.

Heat and humidity: NC State's description says 'Hairy alumroot is heat- and humidity-tolerant' and lists Heat and Humidity under Resistance To Challenges. MoBot says it 'seems to do better in hot and humid summers than most heucheras'. RHS says it 'may be more tolerant of heat and humidity than others, but less tolerant of dry spells'. These are tolerance statements, recorded only as stated; they are not humidity_need, humidity_pct or temperature figures, which are left null.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists all three bands (Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0)), the first two being open-ended, so no closed range is supported. RHS's pH field says Neutral only, with no numeric range.

water_regime and the dry-down/day-interval fields are null: NC State gives only soil tags (Good Drainage, Moist) and a trait that it is moderately drought-tolerant, MoBot's structured Water field is mid-scale (Water: Medium), and RHS gives a Moisture soil descriptor plus Drought Resistance Yes. No admissible source states a watering instruction. Sources also tension on dryness: NC State and MoBot say scorch and decline may occur if soil dries out completely while also calling it drought-tolerant.
soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's bare Good Drainage + Moist pair, RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' and MoBot's 'medium moisture, well-drained' agree; no source asks for wet or boggy soil.

Mature size is taken from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 0 ft. 8 in. - 2 ft. 8 in. = 8-32 in; Width 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in. = 18-24 in). MoBot gives Height 1.50 to 2.50 feet and Spread 1.00 to 2.00 feet (18-30 in by 12-24 in); RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), a coarser band in metres. The sources differ; NC State is the anchor.

chill_damage_f is null: sources give only hardiness zones (NC State 3a-8b, MoBot Zone 3 to 8, RHS H6) and a frost-heaving note, none of which is a damage-onset temperature. Day/night temperature ranges, light_fc, fertilizer fields, cool_rest_note are null: no admissible source states them for this species.

Synonyms: NC State lists Previously known as: Heuchera acerifolia, Heuchera macrorhiza, Heuchera villosa var. macrorhiza. RHS has a separate page for Heuchera villosa var. macrorhiza and lists this species page's name status as Correct; the RHS species page was used here. MoBot has separate pages for cultivars and Heuchera villosa var. atropurpurea; none of those were used. NC State's cultivar notes ('Autumn Bride' etc.) were not used for any field.

NC State is often-confused-with module lists Heuchera sanguinea, which is a different taxon and was not used. No dedicated page on hgic.clemson.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu or fieldreport.caes.uga.edu was found for this exact species (the Clemson factsheet URL tried returned 403), so they contribute nothing.

RHS's Cultivation first sentence ('Grow in a fertile, neutral soil in light or partial shade...') was not used as species evidence because it may be genus-level boilerplate; only the RHS structured fields were cited.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Problems list for Tanacetum parthenium carries these tags: Contact Dermatitis, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy. Separately, NC State's human-scoped "Poisonous to Humans" block gives Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "Airborne dermatitis have been occasionally reported."; Poison Toxic Principle: Parthenin; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. The NC State page lists no poisonous plant part and no pet-specific symptom list. The cat/dog/horse tags are NC State's Problem tags, not part of the human Poison block. RHS, under its "Potentially harmful" heading, adds the handling warning: "Contact may irritate the skin. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". Separately, NC State's Edibility field says "Edible leaves can make tea." with no preparation time or conditions given, and RHS files the plant under "Herbs - Culinary"; these edibility statements sit alongside the low-severity human poison block and contact dermatitis tag above.

toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags; ASPCA is not admissible and not cited. NC State also tags Problem for Horses.

Mature size conflict: NC State gives Height 1-3 ft and Width 1-2 ft (used), while RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in); RHS is not used for size because NC State has the species' own Dimensions block.

water_regime left null: NC State gives only a Moist soil tag, RHS says well-drained and will not tolerate heavy, wet soils; no watering statement. Drought tolerant is a trait, not a watering statement.
